source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.4 opening paragraph: ‘the classical Erdos-Renyi model G(n,p)’
source_evidence.observation: The model is constructed on a set of n vertices by connecting every pair of distinct vertices independently with probability p.

source_evidence.anchor: Figure 2.2 caption and preceding sentence: ‘G ∼ G(n,p)’
source_evidence.observation: The notation G ∼ G(n,p) denotes a random graph sampled from this Erdos-Renyi model.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Proposition 2.4.1: degree d_i is ‘a sum of n − 1 independent Ber(p) random variables (the indicators of the edges incident to i)’
source_evidence.observation: The surrounding application confirms the intended Bernoulli-indicator semantics: each potential incident edge has a Ber(p) indicator, and these edge indicators are independent.

binders: n, the number of vertices [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 opening definition]
p, the common edge-connection probability [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 opening definition]
V, a fixed set of n vertices on which the random graph is constructed [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘on a set of n vertices’]
G, a random graph with distribution G(n,p) [PDF page 10; printed page 21, sentence before Figure 2.2 and its caption]

F, an arbitrary finite family of distinct potential edges, each edge being a pair of distinct vertices, and A ⊆ F, the subfamily prescribed to be present [analyst expansion of the finite joint-independence content of the opening definition on PDF page 10; printed page 21]
hypotheses: n is a vertex count and hence an integer cardinality [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘a set of n vertices’].
p is a valid probability parameter, hence 0 ≤ p ≤ 1 [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘with probability p’].

For every potential edge e (a pair of distinct vertices), its presence indicator is Bernoulli with success probability p [PDF page 10; printed page 21, opening definition; corroborated by the Proposition 2.4.1 proof’s ‘Ber(p) ... indicators of the edges’].

The edge-presence choices for distinct potential edges are jointly independent [PDF page 10; printed page 21, opening phrase ‘connecting every pair of distinct vertices independently’; the finite product formulation uses the standard mutual-independence reading].

The members of F are distinct potential edges and A records exactly those members of F required to be present; members of F \ A are required to be absent [analyst notation for an arbitrary finite edge pattern under the opening definition on PDF page 10; printed page 21].
conclusions: G(n,p) is the random-graph law obtained by deciding independently for every pair of distinct vertices whether to connect that pair, with connection probability p [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 opening definition].

For every potential edge e, P(e is present in G) = p and P(e is absent from G) = 1 − p [PDF page 10; printed page 21, ‘with probability p’; the absence probability is the complementary-event consequence].

For every finite edge family F and prescribed present subfamily A ⊆ F, P(all e ∈ A are present and all e ∈ F \ A are absent) = ∏(e ∈ A) p · ∏(e ∈ F \ A) (1 − p) = p^|A| (1 − p)^|F \ A| [finite product-law expansion of ‘every pair ... independently with probability p’ on PDF page 10; printed page 21].

Equivalently, the edge indicators form a mutually independent family of identically distributed Ber(p) random variables indexed by the potential edges [PDF page 10; printed page 21, opening definition; corroborated by the Proposition 2.4.1 proof].
definitions_and_conventions: A potential edge is indexed by a pair of distinct vertices; in the standard graph reading of the passage, this is one unordered two-element pair, so loops are excluded and there is at most one edge per vertex pair [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘connecting every pair of distinct vertices’].
G ∼ G(n,p) means that G is sampled from the Erdos-Renyi distribution just defined [PDF page 10; printed page 21, sentence before Figure 2.2 and Figure 2.2 caption].
Ber(p) denotes the Bernoulli distribution for an edge-presence indicator [PDF page 10; printed page 21, proof of Proposition 2.4.1].

The product over an empty specified edge family is 1; thus the empty pattern has probability 1 [standard empty-product convention used only to make the finite product-law expansion total; the source does not discuss this case].
implicit_context: The discussion is in a probability text and treats G(n,p) as a probability distribution on graphs [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 introduction and notation G ∼ G(n,p)].
The vertex set is fixed and has cardinality n, but the passage does not prescribe a particular labeling such as {1,…,n} [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘on a set of n vertices’].

The term ‘independently’ is understood in its standard probabilistic sense of mutual independence of the whole edge-indicator family, which yields every finite joint product law [PDF page 10; printed page 21, opening definition].

The model uses a common parameter p for every potential edge, so the edge indicators are identically distributed as well as independent [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘every pair ... with probability p’].

details: The random object is a graph on a fixed n-vertex set [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 opening definition].
Random choices are indexed by pairs of distinct vertices, interpreted as the potential edges [PDF page 10; printed page 21, same definition].
Every potential edge is present with the same probability p [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘every pair ... with probability p’].
The surrounding proof identifies edge indicators as Ber(p) variables [PDF page 10; printed page 21, proof of Proposition 2.4.1].
Distinct edge choices are mutually independent under the standard reading of ‘connecting every pair ... independently’ [PDF page 10; printed page 21, opening definition].

Consequently every finite prescribed present/absent pattern has the product probability p for each required present edge and 1 − p for each required absent edge [finite product-law expansion of the same opening definition].
The product law remains meaningful at p = 0 and p = 1; the passage states no exclusion of these valid probability endpoints [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘probability p’].
For an empty specified family the product is empty and equals 1 by convention; this boundary case is not discussed in the source [standard product convention].

undebatable_constraints: The graph is built on a set containing n vertices [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 opening definition].
Only pairs of distinct vertices are candidates for connection, so no loop choice is part of the model [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘pair of distinct vertices’].
Every potential edge uses the same connection probability p [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘every pair ... with probability p’].
Edge choices are independent [PDF page 10; printed page 21, phrase ‘connecting every pair ... independently’].
Edge-presence indicators have Bernoulli(p) law [PDF page 10; printed page 21, proof of Proposition 2.4.1].

Any faithful explicit edge-pattern formulation must cover simultaneous requirements that some selected edges are present and other selected edges are absent, with one factor p or 1 − p per specified edge [finite joint-product content of the opening definition on PDF page 10; printed page 21].
No additional dependence, unequal edge probabilities, loops, or randomization of the vertex set is part of this stated G(n,p) construction [PDF page 10; printed page 21, opening definition].

ambiguities.issue: The passage does not explicitly say ‘unordered pair,’ ‘simple graph,’ or ‘labeled graph.’
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10; printed page 21 says only ‘on a set of n vertices’ and ‘connecting every pair of distinct vertices.’
ambiguities.impact: The standard graph-theoretic reading is one undirected, loopless edge per unordered pair; a formulation using ordered pairs, directed edges, multiple edges, or loops would require source support not present here. A particular labeling of the fixed vertex set is inessential to the probability law.

ambiguities.issue: The admissible domains of n and p are not written as formal inequalities in the cited paragraph.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10; printed page 21 calls n the number of vertices and p a probability but states no explicit n ≥ 0 or 0 ≤ p ≤ 1 formula.
ambiguities.impact: The natural inherited domains are an integer vertex cardinality and p in [0,1]. Small n, endpoint probabilities, and the empty edge family create only degenerate cases; the source gives no exception excluding them.

ambiguities.issue: The finite edge-pattern product formula is not displayed verbatim in the source.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10; printed page 21 gives the verbal construction ‘connecting every pair of distinct vertices independently with probability p’; the later proof describes incident-edge indicators as independent Ber(p) variables.
ambiguities.impact: The formula p^|A|(1−p)^|F\A| is the exact finite joint-distribution expansion of the stated independent Bernoulli construction, rather than an additional modeling assumption. It requires ‘independently’ to have its standard mutual-independence meaning, not merely pairwise independence.

contract_plain_english: On a fixed set of n vertices, the Erdos-Renyi graph G(n,p) is formed by making one independent Bernoulli(p) decision for each pair of distinct vertices [PDF page 10; printed page 21, Section 2.4 opening definition, corroborated by the Proposition 2.4.1 proof]. Therefore, for any finite collection of distinct candidate edges and any prescribed pattern, the probability of seeing exactly the requested present/absent statuses on that collection is the product of p over requested-present edges and 1 − p over requested-absent edges, equivalently p^a(1 − p)^b. The source leaves the standard undirected/simple-graph convention, the formal domains of n and p, and empty/degenerate cases implicit.
